content.text: Explain the different types of concurrent ownership

Three main types of concurrent ownership: (1) TENANCY IN COMMON - default form; each tenant has undivided interest, freely transferable; no survivorship; can have unequal shares. (2) JOINT TENANCY - requires four unities (time, title, interest, possession); right of survivorship; severable by transfer (becomes TIC with transferee). (3) TENANCY BY THE ENTIRETY - only for married couples; requires fifth unity of marriage; right of survivorship; cannot be severed unilaterally; creditors of one spouse cannot reach. For estate planning: joint tenancy avoids probate but loses step-up in basis on first death; TIC allows different treatment in wills; TBE provides creditor protection. California is community property - spouses have equal undivided interests; can hold as CP with right of survivorship.

Easements can terminate by: (1) RELEASE - written release from easement holder. (2) MERGER - when dominant and servient estates come under single ownership. (3) ABANDONMENT - physical act + intent to abandon (nonuse alone insufficient). (4) PRESCRIPTION - servient owner's adverse, hostile use for statutory period. (5) NECESSITY ENDS - if easement by necessity, terminates when necessity ends. (6) DESTRUCTION - involuntary destruction of servient tenement (doesn't apply to land). (7) CONDEMNATION - government takes servient estate. (8) ESTOPPEL - servient owner changes position in reasonable reliance on statements/conduct by easement holder. (9) EXPIRATION - if easement created for limited time/purpose. Note: easements run with the land unless properly terminated - critical for title searches in estate transfers.
